ECE 6390 / Digital signals

Amplifier & backoff

From the figure to the physics

Fig. 1 shows how reducing amplifier drive trades distortion against output power.

The toy amplifier limits complex amplitude radially: zout = zin/max(1, |zin|). It preserves phase while clipping points above unit amplitude. The input alphabet starts with average symbol energy 1.

Input power backoff IBO in dB scales amplitudes by 10^(−IBO/20) and powers by 10^(−IBO/10). Output backoff uses the resulting mean output power relative to the stated saturation power.

Constellation points reveal amplitude-dependent distortion at symbol instants. Pulse-shaped waveforms can have additional between-symbol peaks; real amplifiers can also introduce phase distortion and memory. Those effects need a waveform and hardware model.

Example

A point with input magnitude 1.2 is limited to magnitude 1. A 3 dB input power backoff multiplies every input amplitude by approximately 0.708 and approximately halves input power.

    Practice

    1. Why does zero clipping of QPSK constellation points fail to establish zero distortion for a pulse-shaped QPSK waveform?

    The plotted points sample symbol instants, while the amplifier sees the complete continuous waveform.

    Filtering and pulse overlap can create peaks between symbol instants. Those peaks can exceed the amplifier limit even when the symbol-center points lie within it.
